title: The Gita at Walden
hook: he bathed his mind in the Bhagavad Gita and imagined Walden's water mingling with the Ganges (Walden 16)

segments.voice: Yesterday, winter animals: owls, barking foxes, chickadees at the corn, and one trembling hare. Your line was winter life. Where did something move in a place that looked empty? Day one thousand two hundred forty.

What could a small New England pond have to do with a river on the other side of the earth? In the winter Thoreau describes, an ice company came to Walden with horses, saws and long tools, cutting the frozen pond into blocks and stacking them high on the shore. The ice would be packed and shipped, he tells us, to hot cities a world away. He watched them work. Then he went back to his cabin, and his book, and his well. And somewhere between the ice saws and the bucket, an answer arrived.
screen: `ICE CUTTERS ON THE POND.` → `SHIPPED TO HOT CITIES.` → `A POND AND A FAR RIVER.`

segments.voice: First, the book. Near the end of The Pond in Winter, Thoreau tells us what he reads in the morning: "In the morning I bathe my intellect in the stupendous and cosmogonal philosophy of the Bhagvat Geeta." That's his spelling of the Bhagavad Gita, the Hindu scripture where Krishna counsels the warrior Arjuna. Notice the verb. Not study. Not skim. Bathe. The way you'd step into the pond. Second, the well. He puts down the book, he says, and goes to his well for water, and there, in his imagination, he meets the servant of a Brahmin priest who sits in his temple on the Ganges reading the Vedas. The two of them, he says, draw water from the same well, and their buckets grate together. A scripture read at dawn has turned a chore into a meeting. Third, the ice. Thoreau thinks of the blocks cut from Walden and shipped away to hot cities in India, among other places, and he writes: "The pure Walden water is mingled with the sacred water of the Ganges." It's a picture of water traveling. It's also a picture of ideas traveling, the other way, from the Ganges to a cabin in Massachusetts. Fourth, what he's doing. Thoreau doesn't claim the Gita as his, or say what Hindus should make of it. He treats it as a neighbor's well he's been allowed to drink from. A line from far away came into his ordinary morning and changed the size of it. His small pond, read beside a great river, didn't feel small anymore.
screen: `I BATHE MY INTELLECT.` · `THE SERVANT AT THE WELL.` · `WALDEN WATER IN THE GANGES.` · then, large: `A NEIGHBOR'S WELL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read a line from far away. Bring to mind one line from a tradition, a land or a language far from your own. It might be something you've heard on this path, or something a friend once said that came from their grandmother's world. If nothing comes, borrow Thoreau's: the pure Walden water is mingled with the sacred water of the Ganges. Settle, and breathe. Let the line sit in you like water. Don't analyze it. Just let it be the morning bath. The bell holds the time.
The Gita at Walden. Thoreau bathed his mind in the Bhagavad Gita in the mornings, and pictured his pond's water mingling with the Ganges. Today's word.

Your line: the ganges and walden. Today, when you drink a glass of water, let it remind you of one line or one person from far away who has become part of your ordinary day. Day one thousand two hundred forty.

howItsDone: Hindus read the Bhagavad Gita as scripture; Thoreau, writing as a reader from outside the tradition, describes bathing his mind in it each morning and picturing Walden's water mingling with the Ganges.

fork.setup: you watch your pond's ice being cut and shipped to hot cities far away. back at your cabin with your morning book, what does Thoreau picture?
options: the ice melting uselessly in a ship's hold.
Walden's water mingling with the sacred water of the Ganges.
the money the ice company will make.
fork.reveal: he pictured the waters meeting, and at his own well, a Brahmin's servant drawing water beside him.

original.note: Sanskrit, from the Hindu tradition: the Bhagavad Gita, rendered in English as 'the song of the Lord'. Thoreau spelled it Bhagvat Geeta.

trapdoor: what you thought: Thoreau dipped into the Gita out of curiosity.
what it means: he made the Gita part of his ordinary mornings, and pictured two waters meeting.
what a scholar hears: The Pond in Winter turns the ice trade into an image of exchange: Walden ice goes east, and the Gita comes west to the well.

notes: Confirm exact wording of both Thoreau quotations from The Pond in Winter. The first sentence continues ('since whose composition years of the gods have elapsed, and in comparison with which our modern world and its literature seem puny and trivial'); the script stops before the comparison, so as not to rank anyone's literature or tradition.

Paraphrased: 'I lay down the book and go to my well for water, and lo! there I meet the servant of the Bramin, priest of Brahma and Vishnu and Indra, who still sits in his temple on the Ganges reading the Vedas... I meet his servant come to draw water for his master, and our buckets as it were grate together in the same well.' Confirm.
The script says the ice went to hot cities 'in India, among other places'; the text names Charleston and New Orleans along with Madras, Bombay and Calcutta. Confirm.

A Hindu Keeper should check the one-line description of the Gita (Krishna counsels the warrior Arjuna) and the gloss 'the song of the Lord' in the original note, and the Devanagari spelling and pronunciation guide.
The ice company's horses and tools are a light paraphrase of Thoreau's description of the ice-cutters; Thoreau gives a number of men, which the script omits.

Editor pass: hook now opens with a question instead of a third winter-on-the-pond scene in a row (after days 1234 and 1239); trapdoor no longer calls the Gita 'exotic'; the original note drops 'often'.
